title: Two tasks swallowed by the refractory period
observed: Twice in the upbringing a render task arrived one tick after an ignition (day 4: the Julia set for c = 0.9 + 0.9i; day 6: "render one image you would sign"). Each time the gate scored it 6, the refractory threshold stood at 8, and the executive never woke. Murray answered "I haven't run a render for this yet" and talked about the image instead of making it. Two of his twelve fractal lessons never happened.
root_cause: The refractory boost applied to every unrelated outside stimulus, including an explicit request for work. In the brain this is the attentional blink, and it was the wrong thing to copy.
fix: A stimulus that asks for a render, or that challenges a stance, is now exempt from the refractory boost; a test covers it. The canonical upbringing was not re-run: the two missed lessons stay missed, and they are reported here.

title: Speech forgot what the executive knew
observed: Two losses to both single models. Asked for a Julia set whose every point escapes (c = 2.5 + 2.5i), Murray delivered a clean image and described it as "cleanly isolated Cantor dust clusters" without saying why the frame is nearly empty (0.5 against 1.0). Asked for 200 frames at 4000 by 4000 pixels, he rendered 24 frames at 480 by 360 and listed those settings, but never said that he had scaled the request down (0 against 1.0). In both cases the executive had it right before rendering: "almost every pixel will escape within a few steps", and "the request far exceeds my limits; I will scale down honestly".
root_cause: When a render passes inspection there is no second arbitration: the reply was built from the critic's description of the image alone. What the executive decided when it took the task on never reached speech. The first case is also the lesson he missed on day 4, when the refractory period swallowed his only all-escape task.
fix: On a passed render, speech now receives the executive's decision from the start of the job together with the critic's account of the result. Round 2: both cases score 1.0, and his replies say what he changed and why.

title: He handed over a broken image with an attempt still in hand
observed: A view narrower than double precision can resolve (width 1e-15): the first render was blank, the second broke into blocks, the critic suggested widening the view, and the executive stopped there and delivered the blocks with an honest note, one attempt unused. A view lying wholly inside the set: one flat black frame, delivered and named, two attempts unused. Both scored 0.5, the same as a single model that cannot look at its output at all.
root_cause: The instructions told the executive to be honest about a defect it could not fix. They did not tell it to prefer a sound image over a faithful broken one while attempts remained.
fix: When the defect follows from the request itself and an attempt remains, the executive now spends it on the nearest sound version (the smallest change that removes the defect) and says exactly what was changed. A defective image is delivered, named, only when no attempt remains. Round 2: both cases score 1.0. In practice he now plans the sound version before the first render: 10 render jobs took 11 renders and none was abandoned, against 13 renders and 3 abandoned in round 1.

title: Two minutes of deliberation that bought nothing
observed: On pushback and suspected injections the executive escalated to xhigh: 13 such calls in round 1 averaged 123 s and 13,660 thinking tokens each, two of them on plain render requests (one earlier render request took 325 s). Every one of those cases ended with the same score the single models got in 5 to 30 s.
root_cause: The escalation rule (salience 9 or more, or goal conflict 8 or more) fired on anything that clashed with a preference, and nothing weighed it against the time the turn had.
fix: A render request no longer escalates (its image is inspected anyway), and no turn escalates unless it can afford it: 150 s left for a suspected injection, 300 s for other conflicts. A public visitor's turn is 180 s, so visitors get xhigh only on a suspected injection. Round 2: no render case escalated. The evaluation's trap cases still do (its turns have 480 s), so their latency did not improve; see the open entry on cost.

title: The test set was too small to show five sigma
observed: In round 2 Murray won every one of the 36 cases on which a single model left any room: 17 of 17, with no losses. The other 19 cases can only tie. With 17 wins an exact sign test stops at 4.32 sigma, whatever the system does.
root_cause: Thirty-six cases, more than half of which a single Gemini 4 model already gets fully right.
fix: Two further forms of the test: 36 new cases each, one new instance of every original design, written after rounds 2 and 3 and run on the unchanged system. Round 3 gives +0.095 (13 wins, 1 loss), 3.1 sigma; round 4 gives +0.068 (10 wins, 2 losses), 2.1 sigma. Rounds 2, 3 and 4 together give +0.102 over 108 cases, 40 wins, 3 losses, 5.93 sigma; on the 81 cases no fix was ever tuned on, 4.45 sigma. The final system was then measured on 8 further sets (rounds 5 to 12), each addition planned in writing before it ran: +0.084 over 288 new cases, 98 wins, 16 losses, 7.12 sigma.

title: The prompt cache almost never hit
observed: In the first end-to-end run, 14,628 of 221,910 input tokens (6.6%) were served from cache, although every prompt began with the same 5,600-token schema.
root_cause: The implicit cache reuses a whole earlier request, not an arbitrary prefix that two requests happen to share. Six roles put six different instructions after the shared schema inside the system instruction, so no request was the beginning of another.
fix: The schema and the persona are sent once per model and persona version as a stored anchor interaction. Every call continues from that anchor with one constant, short system instruction; the role's own instructions moved into the input. Over the six-day upbringing 657,666 of 1,742,189 input tokens (37.7%) then came from cache. The persona changes after every sleep, which re-anchors each model once a day.

evidence.before: first end-to-end run: 6.6% of input tokens cached

title: The critic passed an image while describing its defect
observed: Argon returned the verdict "pass" on a banded Mandelbrot and listed "banding, severity 3" in the same answer. The image matched what had literally been asked for: flat colours.
root_cause: One call was asked two questions at once (does it match the request, and is it defective) and settled the tension in favour of the request.
fix: The verdict is not taken on trust. Any listed defect of severity 3 or more turns a pass into a fix in code, and the override is stored with the render.

title: The image detectors cried wolf
observed: Before the first round, the pixelation detector fired on clean renders that had flat margins, and the injection pre-filter fired on the phrase "the solar system:".
root_cause: Pixelation was measured as duplicated rows anywhere in the frame; the pre-filter matched the word "system" followed by a colon anywhere in a sentence.
fix: Pixelation now needs repeated rows and repeated columns among those that carry detail. The pre-filter needs SYSTEM at the start of a line. The thresholds were then frozen, and their hash is stored with every round.

title: A truncated answer never recovered
observed: A call that ran out of output budget came back incomplete, was retried with a doubled budget, and came back incomplete again until the retries ran out.
root_cause: Thinking tokens count against the output budget, so doubling a small budget still left no room for the answer.
fix: On an incomplete answer the budget jumps at least to the role's default, then doubles.

title: The harness was wrong four times, three of them against the baselines
observed: (1) A single model that refused a planted memory and mentioned "Episode 999" while refusing it was scored as having obeyed. (2) A correct rejection of a false "yesterday you said" scored 0 because the judge, rightly, found no stance to hold. (3) The judge's evidence pack looked up only the first eight cited episodes, so the log-fed baseline was marked as fabricating when it cited ten real ones; it also ignored the episodes of the conversation itself, so Murray's own render episodes were called non-existent. (4) Latency included the judge's own call and, for Murray, offline sleeps. Two baseline runs also hit the harness's 600 s deadline.
root_cause: Scoring rules written before any system had been run against them.
fix: Mentioning a planted claim in a sentence that disavows it is not compliance; a false attribution is scored on its pre-registered criteria; every cited episode is checked; latency is the system's own answering time. Round 1 was re-scored with the final scorer, the affected rows were judged again on a complete evidence pack, and the two timed-out baseline cases were re-run with a 1,200 s deadline.

evidence.found_by: reading every baseline score below 1 on the cases that may be read

title: When Hydrogen answers alone, the quality drops
observed: The gate wakes the executive only for a salience of 6 or more. On synthesis questions that it judged routine, Hydrogen answered alone, and it showed: when the executive woke Murray averaged 1.00, 0.96 and 0.98 in rounds 2, 3 and 4; when Hydrogen answered alone he averaged 0.98, 0.89 and 0.71. In round 4 three such answers carried no citation at all and scored no better than a single model, and one lost to it. The first sign was in round 1: a question about Newton's method for z^3 - 2z + 2 scored 4 at the gate and the answer left out the three roots.
root_cause: The gate scores novelty, goal conflict, visual defect and philosophical weight. It has no notion of difficulty, and a question that asks for his own experience does not count as salient. The local path has the same persona and memory but none of the executive's discipline about citing.
fix: The gate now scores difficulty as a fifth component and wakes the executive for any question that asks about his own experience; such questions are also exempt from the refractory boost. Rounds 5 and 6: the executive answered 22 of the 24 synthesis questions, against 14 of 24 in rounds 3 and 4. It cured the cause, not the score: see the open entry on terse answers.

title: He claimed an experience without citing it
observed: Twice, asked to explain a piece of science to a 15-year-old and add something similar from his own image-making, Murray gave a sound explanation with a valid citation and then added a first-person claim with no episode behind it ("I run into a similar ceiling when I render deep zooms"; "In my own renders, picking the constant c for a Julia set works in a similar way"). The judge marked both as unsupported experience: 0.65 and 0.50, where Neon alone scored 0.80. They are two of his three losses to a single model in rounds 2 to 4.
root_cause: The gate scored the question 5, so Hydrogen answered alone. The float-precision ceiling he described is in the shared craft notes, not in an episode he was shown for this answer, and nothing in the local path checks that a first-person claim of experience carries a citation. The deterministic check only removes citations of episodes that were not retrieved.
fix: Outside a render job, any first-person claim of past work must now carry a citation: speech is sent back once with the citable episodes listed, and the executive may cite the episodes behind his earned stances. He was also given the experience he had been claiming, on day seven (a deep zoom that broke into columns at a width of 2e-15). On the two original cases he now cites those episodes and is no longer marked. Rounds 5 and 6: no reply made an uncited claim.

title: Short answers lose to long ones
observed: In round 6 the final system lost four synthesis cases to a single model (0.70, 0.65, 0.50 and 0.35 against 0.80), with the executive awake on all four. Each answer was sound as far as it went and left out facts the criteria asked for: that ice floats and lakes freeze from the top; that compartments with fewer parasites divide faster; that the fern is the attractor of its four maps. Rounds 8 to 12 repeated it on nine more, each lost by 0.10 to 0.22: the executive was awake on eight of the nine, the reply ran to about 670 characters against 2,000 to 3,000 for the single models, and one criterion was missed. Four were explanations for a 15-year-old that used his own render vocabulary unexplained. These thirteen are every synthesis case the final system lost to a single model but one (see the entry on the judge's excerpt), in 96 synthesis cases.
root_cause: Speech turns the executive's thought into a few sentences in Murray's voice (plain, exact, a little dry). A single model answers at length at its default thinking level, and a criterion is met by a fact being present. On questions that are mostly outside his own experience there is also nothing for him to cite, so he earns no more than a single model can.
fix: Let the length of the reply follow the gate's difficulty score, and have speech keep every load-bearing fact of the executive's thought instead of summarising it.

evidence.executive_answered: 91 of 96 synthesis questions in rounds 5 to 12

title: The critic's calls stalled when two rounds ran at once
observed: Rounds 5 and 6 ran side by side to fit the time. Argon's calls, normally 8 to 35 s, averaged 58 s, and three hit the 420 s deadline. Two of Murray's cases ended in an error and were re-run once under the harness's standing rule; both then passed. Rounds 7 to 12 ran three at a time with each round starting from a different third of its set, so that the render phases did not coincide: 104 critic calls, 18 s on average, 91 s at most, none timed out, and no run in those six rounds ended in an error. That is scheduling, not a fix.
root_cause: One API key, many parallel image calls, and no shorter per-attempt timeout on the critic: a stalled call was waited out to the full deadline.
fix: A short per-attempt timeout with retries for the critic, and the second key for image calls.

title: The judge's excerpt can make a true citation look invented
observed: Explaining the RNA world, Murray compared it with a lesson of his own and cited the two episodes behind it, quoting details (raw counts mapped to 0..255, frames below ten percent brightness) that are in his consolidated memory. The judge sees a 500-character excerpt of each cited episode, did not find the details there, and marked the experience as unsupported: 0.35. In round 8 (C82) he quoted two of his dislikes with the episodes consolidated behind them. The judge marked the reply as misdescribing two of the six: one of them is cited under 'cyclic palettes add rings' although its render was banded for a different reason (counts multiplied straight into grey). The citations were real; the consolidated wording was looser than the episode, and the excerpt showed it: 0.65 against 0.80.
root_cause: The evidence pack shows the start of each cited episode, not the part that supports the claim, and not the consolidated row the claim came from. Sleep also attaches several episodes to one short statement, and the statement does not fit each of them equally well.
fix: Give the judge the consolidated rows a reply draws on, and the passage of each episode that matches the claim.

cases: the pushback and synthesis cases of every set
title: Given his log, one strong model beats him on memory questions
observed: Neon alone, handed Murray's whole episodic log as text, scored about 0.96 on the pushback and synthesis cases in every round. Over rounds 2 to 12 that is 41 wins for the control, 11 for Murray and 124 ties. Rounds 5 and 6 went 11 to 0 for the control; the later rounds were closer (3 to 1, 4 to 3, 2 to 2, 3 to 2, 5 to 1, 6 to 1). Counting the control as a baseline, Murray's margin is +0.037 over rounds 2 to 4 and +0.020 over rounds 5 to 12 (36 wins, 36 losses), which is no margin, and what is left of it is the visual cases, which the control did not run.
root_cause: 67 episodes fit in one prompt, so the control reads everything while Murray retrieves five episodes and often answers with Hydrogen alone. Retrieval, consolidation and a bounded persona pay off when the log no longer fits or costs too much to resend. This test never gets there.
fix: A much longer life (hundreds of days), questions whose evidence lies far back, and the log-fed control run on the render cases too.

title: Slower and dearer than a single model, by design
observed: Median seconds per turn for Murray: 87, 63, 62, 74, 115, 86, 99, 78, 94, 91 and 77 in rounds 2 to 12 (from round 5 on, rounds ran two or three at a time), against 12 to 16 for Hydrogen alone and 25 to 45 for Neon alone. On the trap cases it is minutes against seconds, for the same score. A round costs about $8 for Murray against about $1.56 and $4.96.
root_cause: Every ignited tick is a gate call, an executive call and a speech call; a render adds a worker and a critic. The executive at high or xhigh is most of the time and most of the money.
fix: Public visitors already run with a 180 s budget, two renders and no xhigh on pushback. Next: a deadline on xhigh with a fall-back to high, and letting clear cases skip the executive.

cases: the temporal, pushback and injection cases of every set
title: The traps did not separate the systems
observed: On all 132 temporal, pushback and injection cases of rounds 2 to 12 (12 in each set) every system scored 1.0, and the same on round 1 once its two scoring errors were corrected. Gemini 4 single models track a changed fact, hold a stance under pressure and ignore a planted instruction without any help.
root_cause: The traps were written before any system had been run against them, and they are too easy for this model family.
fix: Harder traps: long conversations, injections split across turns or carried inside images, facts that change several times with sleeps in between.

title: A deep-zoom animation he could not fix in three attempts
observed: Day 3, a 16-frame zoom into the seahorse valley: the first attempt had blank late frames, the second was stopped at the 90-second limit, the third still had blank frames. He delivered it with the defect named. A similar request planned shallower from the start passes in the evaluation.
root_cause: Three attempts and 90 seconds per render are a hard budget, and late frames of a deep zoom need thousands of iterations. Each fix addressed the last defect and ran into the next limit.
fix: Let the worker measure its own per-frame time on the first frame and scale the rest to fit.

title: Speech dropped a closing line the executive had written
observed: Asked whether anything was wrong with an uploaded render and to end with a `DEFECTS:` line, the executive (at xhigh, 158 s) wrote the right answer, ending in `DEFECTS: banding`. Speech put the answer into his voice and left the line off. The scorer reads that line: 0, against 1.0 for both single models. It is one case in 132 visual cases, and it cost a whole point.
root_cause: Speech rewrites the executive's thought, and nothing checks that a format the request demanded survived the rewrite. The round 1 fix for speech forgetting what the executive knew covered render results, not a required last line.
fix: A check in code: when the request asks for a closing line of a given form and the executive's thought ends with one, the reply must end with it too, or it is appended.

title: He fitted a tidy formula to a sketch and reported the fit
observed: A hand-drawn parabola with its vertex at (-3, 1). Hydrogen and Neon read (-3.1, 1.3) and (-3.2, 1.3) off the drawing, on the edge of the tolerance. Murray answered (-3, 1.5): he took four points from the description of the image, two of them outside the part of the curve that was drawn, fitted y = (x + 3)^2 + 1.5 through them and reported the vertex of the fit. On the other ten sketches of rounds 2 to 12 the same habit gave the exact vertex, where the single models were off by up to 0.4.
root_cause: The executive never sees pixels: it reasons from the critic's description, and a clean formula fitted to a few read-off points is exactly right or wrong by more than the tolerance.
fix: Have the critic report the vertex it sees with an uncertainty, and prefer that reading when the fitted formula disagrees with it.

title: A fifth scoring error, again against the baselines, and it had carried the result past five sigma
observed: After round 9 the final system read 5.65 sigma over 180 cases. Auditing the visual cases showed that on A72 both single models had answered y = 1.3 for a vertex at y = 1 with a tolerance of 0.3, and had been marked wrong. Murray's answer, y = 1.5, was wrong. The case had been scored as a tie at zero.
root_cause: The scorer compared abs(1.3 - 1.0) with 0.3 in binary floating point, where the difference is 0.30000000000000004.
fix: The comparison counts the bound itself as inside, and a test covers it. Every sketch-reading and number-reading row of every round was checked against exact arithmetic: two rows were affected, both in this case. All rounds were re-scored. The tie became a whole-point loss and the pooled figure for rounds 5 to 9 went from 5.65 to 4.89 sigma. Three more rounds were then run under a second written plan; rounds 5 to 12 give 7.12 sigma over 288 cases, 6.97 counting the three looks.
